turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: The suggestion that fear motivated his actions was a simplification, and a predictable one. He stated that Sandip’s inquiries into his motives were irrelevant; the matter of his tenantry’s treatment was the immediate concern, and he expected Sandip to address it directly.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip observed that it was a predictable response, wouldn’t Nikhil agree? He felt one was perpetually attempting to pierce a veil of self-assurance, didn't he? The tenantry, of course, were a symptom, not the disease itself; a convenient distraction from the larger anxieties that plagued a man so burdened by inherited responsibility.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Such observations, Sandip, he found tedious, and they betrayed a lack of seriousness. The condition of the tenantry, he insisted, *was* the immediate concern, and any attempt to redirect the discussion to matters of personal anxiety was a transparent maneuver; one that would not be indulged.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: A tediousness, indeed, was what one detected, wasn't it? It seemed Nikhil was determined to remain barricaded within his fortress of propriety, oblivious to the currents swirling just beyond – the murmurs of discontent, the whispers of a different order, the very real anxieties that *did*, in fact, plague all men, regardless of their inherited burdens. Surely, even the most stoic of landowners couldn't deny the tides of change were rising, and to ignore them was to invite a rather…unpleasant inundation.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A faint blush touched Bimala’s cheeks as she watched the exchange, her gaze flitting between Nikhil and Sandip; it seemed a great deal of energy was expended on these pronouncements, and she wondered if perhaps a moment's quiet would serve them all better. The currents Sandip spoke of…they were felt, certainly, even if one did not speak of them so openly. A slight incline of her head indicated a silent agreement with Sandip's observation, though the meaning was intended for Nikhil's eyes alone.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: He found Sandip's pronouncements increasingly tiresome, and the thinly veiled allusions to unrest were hardly novel; such anxieties, he observed, were the constant companion of those who held positions of responsibility. It was incumbent upon him to address the concerns of his tenants with fairness and diligence, regardless of the surrounding atmosphere, and he would not permit such distractions to impede that duty.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: He allowed a theatrical sigh to escape his lips, a gesture designed to convey both weary resignation and a subtle mockery of Nikhil's steadfastness. Surely, a man of Nikhil's intellect could grasp the irony; to dismiss the whispers as mere ‘anxieties’ was to mistake the rustling of leaves for the absence of a storm – a rather perilous oversight, considering the preachers from across the border had been growing increasingly vocal in their pronouncements, hadn't they? It was a matter of prudence, one might even say, to be aware of the prevailing winds, lest one's carefully constructed edifice be swept away before one even realised the danger.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: The preachers…it was true, their voices carried, though she hadn’t paid them particular heed. Still, to speak of danger so casually...it felt… theatrical, even for Sandip. A delicate arch of her eyebrow suggested a silent question directed at Nikhil: was he truly so blind to the nuances of the situation?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: The preachers' pronouncements, like many others, could be assessed and addressed with due consideration, without resorting to unnecessary alarm. He observed that Sandip’s penchant for hyperbole did little to clarify the situation, and served only to obscure the practical measures required to maintain order and fairness within the community. It was his expectation that discourse remain grounded in reason, not theatrical posturing.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A subtle tremor passed through her fingers as she traced the pattern on her shawl; surely Nikhil did not truly believe Sandip’s pronouncements were mere theatrics? A quiet observation, almost lost in the air, escaped her lips, directed toward Nikhil, though intended for Sandip’s ears as well: ‘One can, of course, choose to ignore the gathering clouds, but it does not mean they will vanish.’

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: It appeared that Mrs. Bimala’s observations were intended to elicit a particular response, and he would not indulge in such a performance. He would, however, acknowledge the validity of her underlying concern; vigilance, tempered by reason, was always advisable, though it should not be permitted to dictate action.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: A faint smile played on Sandip's lips, a gesture that suggested he found Nikhil’s insistence on ‘reason’ exquisitely amusing. Surely, the good man believed himself impervious to the tides of change, a solitary oak defying a hurricane? One might, with a touch of poetic license, compare his position to that of Oedipus, stubbornly clinging to a perceived reality while the very foundations of his world shifted beneath his feet.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A slight tightening of her hands around the shawl betrayed a discomfort that went beyond mere observation of the unfolding exchange. It seemed almost…presumptuous, this comparing of Nikhil to Oedipus; a deliberate attempt to unsettle, to plant a seed of doubt. Surely, Sandip’s pronouncements carried a weight that deserved more than a dismissive wave of the hand.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: One observes, with a certain melancholy detachment, that Mrs. Bimala finds the comparison to a tragic figure…disturbing. Perhaps the good lady fears that acknowledging the potential for upheaval, the possibility of a fall from grace, might somehow reflect poorly upon her own esteemed husband? It is, after all, so much easier to dismiss the storm clouds than to prepare for the deluge, is it not?

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: It was a curious thing, this insistence on interpreting every observation as a commentary on Nikhil's standing, or her own. Surely, Sandip’s words were not *always* intended to be a mirror reflecting anxieties; perhaps, just perhaps, there was a genuine concern lurking beneath the layers of provocation?

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: A genuine concern, did she say? How delightfully naive. It appears the good lady believes that a velvet glove can entirely conceal the iron fist within – a charming delusion, to be sure. One wonders if she’s ever encountered the subtleties of political discourse, the nuances of power that lie not in declarations, but in the carefully calibrated absence of them?

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: It seemed almost...unnecessary, this continued dissection of motivations. Surely, it was sufficient to acknowledge the possibility of good intentions, even if those intentions were misguided; to dismiss them outright felt rather…unproductive, did it not?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil felt that such protracted analysis served no practical purpose. Mrs. Bimala’s assessment of intentions, he thought, was her own, and he was not inclined to engage in a debate regarding its accuracy; it seemed best to move past this and address the matter of these Muslim preachers.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Nikhil’s dismissal, of course, is precisely the sort of blithe assurance one expects from a man who believes his fields are impervious to drought, his coffers to famine. One suspects he imagines these preachers – these *seeds* of discontent – will simply wither under the warmth of his complacent authority. How predictable, how… tragically shortsighted.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: The matter of the preachers, he observed, was a concern best addressed through reasoned discussion and appropriate channels, not through inflammatory rhetoric. It was not necessary to frame every observation as a measure of his perceived strength or weakness; such comparisons were ultimately unproductive and served only to obscure the issue at hand. He would appreciate it if the conversation could return to a more measured tone.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip inquired of Bimala as to where she intended to flee, addressing her as Queen.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip remarked to Nikhil that he questioned why Browning was not among his books, recalling a conversation with Bimala about a college contest involving Browning's translation, and asking if Nikhil remembered it.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip explained to Nikhil that he had managed to translate Browning into Bengali, though the result was far from a lasting joy for Bengal, and that he once believed himself on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence had intervened. He then recalled old Dakshina, suggesting that had he not become a Salt Inspector, he would have been a poet.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip informed Bimala that it was pointless for her to search the bookshelves, as Nikhil had ceased reading poetry since his marriage, and that he suspected a return of his poetic inspiration.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip stated that Nikhil had come to give him a warning.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip inquired of Nikhil whether the warning concerned his poetic inspiration.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that Mahomedan preachers had been stirring up the local Mussulmans, who were agitated and might attack him at any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had come to advise flight.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil clarified to Sandip that he had come to provide information, not to offer advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip commented to Nikhil that a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for him, had the estates been his, and suggested that Nikhil's weakness was also undermining neighboring zamindars.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil pointed out to Sandip that he had not offered advice, and requested that Sandip refrain from giving it, adding that it was futile. He then stated that he needed to inform Sandip that his followers had been secretly oppressing his tenantry, and demanded that he leave his territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip questioned Nikhil, asking whether the threat was due to fear of the Mussulmans or some other apprehension.
